That's what it says there and that is one of the weaknesses of the system, because, therefore, the House of Representatives had somewhat broader competencies than is usual and customary in parliamentary systems, whereas I was speaking about the fact that he did not assume the executive functions which the House of Representatives performs in the first stages of existence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, when it was the only body, and not only the legislative body, when the presidency was the sole body and not only a legislative body of that community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, as a constitutional expert, you would have to agree that it is not unusual for the House of Representatives to be the repository of legislative power in any polity, is it?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. Perhaps the interpretation wasn't the right one. I did not maintain anything of the kind. I only said, and I'll say it again, that the House of Representatives assumed legislative, or largely legislative, functions of the former presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and it did not take over those functions which the presidency performed up until the 3rd of July, 1992, while that presidency was the sole organ of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and for as long as, in formal terms, it was not proclaimed the House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the new Croatian republic, sir, there was the office of president, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no office of vice-president, was there, as there had been in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just skip past tabs 4 and 5, which are appointments that speak for themselves. I'd like you to turn to tab 6, please, which is the law on the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna that was signed on September the 30th, 1993, by Perica Jukic. Just a few articles I'd like to bring to your attention. Article 3, sir, specifically provides that the government of this republic is expressly responsible to the House of Representatives, correct, or the Chamber of Deputies?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last article I want to draw to your attention is Article 46, because it helps us peg the date essentially when the civilian functions of the HVO expired. It's true, is it not, sir, that as of September the 30th, 1993, according to Article 46 of the law of the government of this republic, the departments of the HVO would continue their work as ministries of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That shows the continuity. But you have skipped over Article 4, which speaks about relations between the Chamber of Deputies and the government, and where it is stated that the presidents are elected and relieved of duty by the Prime Minister, which is unusual for parliamentary systems, where they are appointed by the head of state following proposals and candidates and nominations for the post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could I ask you to turn to tab 9, sir, which is a declaration on the adoption of documents on the protection and exercise of human freedoms and rights, adopted on September the 30th, 1993, by the new republic. You said, sir, I believe, in your opinion, that to you this was one indicium of the conversion, if you like, of the republic into an independent republic, independent from the state or the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not claim this with respect to document 9, the declaration on the adoption of documents on the protection and exercise of human freedoms and rights, which I assessed positively, in positive terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to agree, sir, that the declaration that you see at tab 9 is precisely the same as Annex C to the Owen-Stoltenberg agreement that we have put on the ELMO. The same agreements are laid out in precisely the same order. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, but let me repeat again that in my study, I say that the declaration is a positive one, and that it is a pity that it was not adopted earlier on, and that it shows a different relationship of Herceg-Bosna towards the protection of human rights and freedoms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Two final questions of detail, sir. If you would look, please, at tab 7 and tab 8. Both of these deal with nominations to two separate commissions of the House of Representatives, one on election and nomination to the House of Representatives or Chamber of Deputies, and one dealing with a commission on appointments -- sorry -- the other one dealing with the committee on internal and foreign policy and national security of the House of Representatives. On September the 30th, 1993, Mr. Kordic was appointed as the president of the first commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Five other members in that commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second commission to which Mr. Kordic was appointed by Perica Jukic was -- consisted of ten members, of whom he was one but not the president; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were ten members and a president, and he was one of the members. In my opinion, the commission --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing I'd like you to take a look at is tab 10, which is the appointments to the government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You're familiar with this document, are you not?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, the president of the HVO, was appointed to be the Prime Minister of the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kordic was not a member of the government of the republic, was he, sir?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next document I'd like you to look at, sir, is tab 11, which is a decision on adopting the presidential council of the republic. There are nine separate members appointed to this council, whose function was to monitor strategic, political, and defence issues, and to coordinate the activities of the republic's executive bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for going back to one of the earlier questions, sir. I asked you whether Mr. Kordic was a member of the government of the republic, and I put it to you that he was not on November the 20th, 1993; that is true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was not a member of the government, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, insofar as the presidential council is concerned, sir, there were nine members, including Lieutenant-General Ante Roso, and Mr. Kordic was not one of the nine members, was he?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next document I would like to draw to your attention is tab 12. It's true, is it not, sir, that Mr. Ivan Bender was appointed as the chairman of the House of Representatives on February the 17th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The two vice-presidents were appointed on the same day, Mr. Kordic being one and Mr. Santic being the other, if you would just consult tab 13; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same day sir, in the last tab, you will see that new appointments were made to the presidential commission, 11 separate members, and Mr. Kordic was not one of them, was he?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Ribicic. My name is Goran Mikulicic, I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and in this case, I represent the second accused, Mario Cerkez, together with Mr. Kovacic. I shall not take as long as my colleague Mr. Sayers, and I shall focus on two topics only. I should like to remind you, Mr. Ribicic, that during your testimony, in the introduction and in your written finding, you spoke about the attributes of state, and then you listed that the attributes of a state are territory, population, a sovereign government, and, according to some legal theoreticians, subordination to international law; that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we were, in observance of this position, to apply it to the emergence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was recognised by the International Community on the 6th of April, 1992 as a sovereign republic, would you agree with me that at that point in time, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not fully control its territory, in view of the formation of the autonomous regions organised by the Serbs in Bosnia, or occupied by them?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. At first, it did not control the part of its territory where the autonomous regions were formed, and afterwards, after the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it did not control that part of its territory either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we focus on the 6th of April, 1992, when the International Community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state, you would agree with me that that was more an expression of the political will of the International Community than a matter of international legality, taking into account these attributes of a state that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an expression of the desire that it should be so and an expression of support to a unified and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the situation in reality was such that two-thirds of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was occupied, in a sense, or rather in a situation of tacit aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will also agree that the capital of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which all the state institutions were based was surrounded by the Serb army and under siege.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that we will agree, Dr. Ribicic, that all these circumstances that we have referred to actually prevented the normal functioning of the state authority of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When speaking about the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have in mind the three constituent peoples: the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats living in the area. Is it right, Dr. Ribicic, that all three peoples in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually have their own specific culture, language, and symbols to which they are emotionally attached?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, if we were to view one of these three entities, that is, the Croatian entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we note that it is not homogeneous in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather that the Croats are living in groups in the Posavina area, bordering on Croatia; in Central Bosnia; and in Herzegovina, on the southern border with Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in other towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you then agree with me that it is not necessary for these three main groups of Croats in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- they could have had different objectives and goals?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the debates about this, how to act, which you described well, Mr. Mikulicic, views differed completely between the Croats living and working in Sarajevo and in other towns, as compared to the proposals as to how things should be done made by those Croats living in the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina bordering on the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we were now to focus on the area of Central Bosnia, that is, the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, and Kiseljak, would you agree with me that this was a kind of enclave of Croats entirely surrounded by majority Muslim entities or settlements?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that is a slight exaggeration, but essentially it is true for the situation at the time, when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Dr. Ribicic, that after the Serb aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina, about 120,000 Muslims fled and came to the area of Central Bosnia where they didn't used to live, provoking an imbalance in the ethnic composition, as compared to the situation before the war?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the policies of the SDS and the formation of Serb autonomous regions was the cause of this resettlement of other peoples from those areas. So the situation must have been difficult in that smaller part of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was not under this tacit occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me, Dr. Ribicic, to remind you of documents shown to you yesterday, P27.2, the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, dated the 18th of November, in Grude. You remember that document. The 18th of November, 1991, in Grude. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, Dr. Ribicic, that representatives of the municipalities were present and that they actually signed this decision on the establishment of the HZ HB. Do you know, Dr. Ribicic, that representing Vitez municipality was the town mayor, Ivan Santic, who refused to sign that document, and that this was done later on, instead of him, by Anto Valenta? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the first part of what you said, that the representative of Vitez municipality did not vote in favour of this decision, and I was not aware of the second part of your statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you knew that Mr. Valenta was a political official of the HDZ, and later the vice-president?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were speaking a moment ago, Dr. Ribicic, about the various peace plans whereby the International Community tried to influence a settlement to the conflict in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mention was made of the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, the Washington and, later, Dayton Agreements.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe the influence of the International Community on developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you could tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my finding, I referred to that briefly, in a number of places in my report, that that influence was certainly quite considerable. Various authors studying these matters have different views as to the extent of that influence. I certainly favourably view that part of the activities of the International Community directed towards international recognition of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the subsequent plans and activities of the International Community, in many respects, it emerged that views among the representatives of the most powerful nations in the world differed so that the influence of their activity varied, in the sense that frequently they did not know how to tackle the problem, and also frequently it appeared as if they were somehow agreeing or accepting the establishment of ethnically homogenous entities within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement that, on the one hand, there was an undisputed influence of the International Community but which was not homogeneous, and, on the other hand, the entities representing the constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not react homogeneously to those proposals?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is correct. In fact, I think they misinterpreted frequently the International Community's advocacy of homogeneous ethnic entities within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like us to comment on the relationship between two states: on the one hand, between the state of the Republic of Croatia, and, on the other, the state of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You said, and we know, that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised on the 6th of April, 1992 as a sovereign state by the International Community. Do you know that on the very next day, on the 7th of April, the Republic of Croatia recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. The late President Franjo Tudjman emphasised this repeatedly. I think the last time was when he was in Sarajevo at a press conference, when he mentioned all the positive elements of Croatia's official support to sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. Among others, he mentioned that element, and I included all those elements in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also know, I assume, Mr. Ribicic, that after that, diplomatic relations were established between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina at an ambassadorial level, that the Croatian ambassador came to Sarajevo, along the well-known tunnel under the airport.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the tunnel, but I know that ambassadors were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume, Dr. Ribicic, that you also know, and evidence has been tendered, D30/2 and D31/2, that in Zagreb, the capital of Croatia, there was an embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the moment it was founded to this day.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also know that attached to that embassy throughout that period, there was a military representative office of the BH army with departments in Zagreb and Split?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just drawing the attention of the Chamber to the fact that I'm referring to Exhibit D31/2, which has already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Ribicic, that you also know that in the period we're referring to, the Republic of Croatia cared for about 450,000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that such aid was extended, though it is another matter why so many refugees crossed the borders and how that could have been prevented in Herceg-Bosna itself and throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also know, Dr. Ribicic, I assume, that a large number of patients and wounded from Bosnia-Herzegovina were treated by the Republic of Croatia in its medical institutions, especially in Split.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, do you also know that on the basis of an agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the possibility was introduced of dual citizenship for citizens of these two states?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, and I also know that many Muslims, even before the beginning of the war, had been granted Croatian citizenship, although they were at the same time citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, do you know of an example when the Croatian parliament, the Sabor, or the government, while the conflict was ongoing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopted a law or any legislation which would discriminate towards the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina by, shall I say, confiscating their property, prohibition on movement, or in any other way discriminating against the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who happened to be in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. On the contrary. I pointed out in my written opinion that the supreme bodies of the Republic of Croatia officially supported the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that Croats were advised at a referendum to vote for the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that the Republic of Croatia was the first to recognise the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that it exchanged ambassadors with it; that weapons for the struggle against aggression and other military aid came, in the first place, from Croatia, and so on. And I have listed all those positive elements of official policy headed by the Croatian assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Fully acknowledging all these circumstances that we have just described, uninterrupted diplomatic relations, the existence of a military representative office of the BH army in Zagreb, the absence of any discriminatory law towards citizens of that state, care for the refugees and the wounded, delivery of humanitarian aid, continuous, uninterrupted contact between political and state representatives between the two countries, in your view, in the period we're discussing, that is, the period from 1992 to 1994, between these two states, the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there a war on at the state level?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking into consideration what the Republic of Croatia did officially and in public, and the decisions it passed in the Croatian Assembly, one could describe those relations as good neighbourly relations between two states. But judging by what part of the leadership of the republic was doing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you. I'm asking you, at the state level and in formal legal terms. On the ground is another matter.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not thinking of the ground, I was thinking of the activities of the state leadership of the Republic of Croatia and only that part of the leadership which were members of the HDZ, those activities were in complete contradiction with this official public state policy. So if we take the assembly decisions, we get a completely different impression than if we take into consideration the political developments where the mentioned part of the Croatian leadership was actually working for a long time on the annexation of a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a division of that republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, this was before the referendum on the sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you're referring to the meeting of the 27th of November in 1992 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is only one of those meetings. There were meetings before that and after that, and activities which were in direct contradiction with the official state policy of the Republic of Croatia towards neighbouring Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Ribicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask, in order to get on with most of it, if we could have a brief private session for the first question that I would like to raise on redirect, and then the rest, of course, will be open session. It pertains to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, I'm going to ask that the usher distribute to you -- there are three documents which I would like to raise. I apologise; there is no translation. These, of course, were taken in response to what was raised on cross, and there are groups of three for, I believe, a significant number of people. The question was asked of you, Dr. Ribicic, concerning whether or not the representatives of the Croat communities were on notice about the Constitutional Court action to be taken by the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You made reference to certain documents. Would you turn, please, to the document that will be presented to you, that will have the HDZ BiH letterhead on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, while we are dealing with this constitutional problem since yesterday, and we've been with it. It's practically the second day of discussion here. But our objective here is not to make a study about these constitutional matters in detail, as I said yesterday. Unfortunately, the cross-examination also started going into detail and into all this documentation, which really has no direct bearing on our case. So will you please try to cut your re-examination shorter and try to focus really on the matter at hand; that is, the analysis of the constitutionalities in this particular case and not constitutionalities as such. We're not here to discuss the constitutional processes involving Herceg-Bosna or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. The point -- if I may just tender the point to the court was that there is -- this is a response to the court, signed by Ivan Markovic, the general secretary of the party, HDZ BiH, indicating essentially that they have -- that their own government is being formed and is pretty much putting off the entire issue of need to address this, and I can certainly provide later for the Court's consideration, but I would ask that the documents go in. They are relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, yesterday there was a question raised to you about whether or not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down, Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday there was a question raised as to whether or not there was any discussion about the actual division of Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the documents of Herceg-Bosna. Are you aware of Karadjordjevo occurring in March 1991? Do you know what that represented?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard about a meeting in Karadjordjevo, a meeting between late President Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic. A great deal has been written about it. There are very many statements about that, and one of the testimonies about it which set out to put -- to bring together in one place all the echoes with which this meeting had and those opinions. So I can give no opinion of my own as to what went on in Karadjordjevo. All that I know is second-hand. But immediately after that meeting, in the wake of that meeting, I heard from colleagues in Croatia that that is where the talks about the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina commenced, at the initiative of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Franjo Tudjman was present. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask the Court to look at and distribute very briefly to Dr. Ribicic Z35.1, which is an opinion of the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would ask Dr. Ribicic, very briefly, because you raised this earlier, to comment on what was asked on 20 November; two days after the founding of Herceg-Bosna, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, what was the issue that was raised by Lord Carrington for the conference on Yugoslavia, and the significance, in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as Badinter's commission is concerned, it -- I did understand you well. You are speaking about the Badinter Commission, are you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the Badinter Commission. And this particular opinion, the opinion number -- the opinion that is present in front of you, the issue about boundaries. If you could comment on that which concerns Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Badinter's commission, it consisted of the highest representatives of constitutional courts of some western countries. And it was of great consequence, not only for Bosnia-Herzegovina but also for other republics -- Slovenia, Croatia, and Macedonia -- because it addressed the dissolution of Yugoslavia rather than the secession of some of the republics. Now, insofar as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, Serbia raised the question whether they -- a same principle could be applied to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers. I am sorry, Mr. Ribicic. Here you have an opinion of the Badinter Commission. Would you please ask a specific question of the witness? Don't ask him about Badinter's commission in general, because that is not the subject of this expert opinion. Ask him a direct question. What do you want to hear from him about this opinion, which is an opinion which we know and which addresses the problems of international law. Which aspect of it do you want answered? You cannot ask such open-ended questions, because we can talk about Badinter's commission for the next four or five hours and so forth. There is a great deal of literature about that commission, and I'm sure you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question that was raised, if could you indicate what is in quotation marks under the paragraph starting "On November 20th, 1991," what is the question is actually addressed?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It addressed the question of boundaries between republics and recognising the boundaries between republics, including the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as internationally recognised borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Ribicic, there was a discussion during cross-examination about an agreement between, among others, Boban and Izetbegovic in Zagreb about the HVO status. I would ask -- it is marked, I believe -- I hope it has been tendered -- as Z2416, but I ask that it be put on the ELMO for one particular point to be raised, and it is the second page of the exhibit which I will need to get back, of course. Yes, second page of it. If you could take a quick look. At whose behest -- who was present at that meeting in Zagreb? There is a list of names, and it is significant that you indicate who is there, please. No, the second page. I'm sorry. The next page. Correct. At the meeting invoked in Zagreb, could you just kindly indicate --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, the meeting was attended by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Mr. Mate Boban, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, the Ambassador Peter Hall, Ambassador Herbert Auken [phoen], Pater Arans [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can stop there. And at the head of it, Lord David Owen, the same person who was involved in the Owen-Stoltenberg and the Vance-Owen Plans. Thank you very much. Moving on. I would ask -- it is -- this has not been -- this has been tendered previously by the Defence. It is the statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It is an HVO binder, tab 2, and just for convenience -- if you have it handy, fine; if not, I'd be happy to have you put it on the ELMO. It is an important point. HVO binder, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 3. And indicate, please, to whom is the HVO and every other member accountable in all instances? To whom?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO, as a whole, and every individual member of the HVO are accountable for the work to the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this, of course, is dealt with as well in your paper. And Article 6, same page. Could you read Article 6, please, briefly?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The HVO shall regulate the activities, structure, operational framework, and powers of its departments, in accordance with the relations passed by the presidency." It is quite clear that the HVO was set up pursuant to the decision of the presidency of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and which also adopted a relevant decision and, therefore, it was responsible for its work to the presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The issue of whether or not Herceg-Bosna could have chosen to use the existing criminal codes of Croatia or of Bosnia. I would like to ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sadly, we have only one copy, because it was -- in response, but if you would put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about the Criminal Code of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher would please put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at that document, Dr. Ribicic, are you able -- which is about the Criminal Code in Croatia, are you able to indicate whether or not there was continuity from the SFRY's Criminal Code, taken by the Republic of Croatia, similar to what was done in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered the Defence's question about it, what it meant to take over the Criminal Code of the Federal state. The same holds true of the Republic of Croatia, that in the Republic of Croatia, in an identical manner, to cover the Federal Criminal Code, like the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And I think the Defence said something else, that in addition to the Federal Criminal Code, it was also possible to take over the Republican Criminal Code, notably, the Croatian. Nevertheless, they took over the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that was the Defence's question. Now, what does this -- what does it mean to take over a law? Well, the law that we have here shows that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna treated the federal and republican legislature in a similar way as the Republic of Croatia; that is, as if it were one of the republics of the former Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Dr. Ribicic, you had begun to comment on certain aspects of the criminal law which I think are significant. You were interrupted during cross-examination. You mentioned -- you seemed to suggest there were certain deficiencies in the criminal law as incorporated into the HR HB legislation with regard to International Humanitarian Law. Would you comment, please, on that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this question. What I was about to say was that in principle, Herceg-Bosna, rather early in the day and in rather general terms, singled out the importance of International Humanitarian Law, but that it did not find its operationalisation in other legal enactments of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, unlike other criminal offences and disciplinary measures -- disciplinary offences in the HVO ranks and so on and so forth. That is what I tried to say, was International Humanitarian Law remained a kind of general commitment, whilst, on the other hand, there were very strict sanctions, down to the death penalty, relating to those offences which covered the non-compliance with orders, failure to carry out the orders of superior officers, and so on and so forth. And that is how we see the discrepancy, the true importance attached to humanitarian law and the other one, because now both things are treated with the same weight. In my report, I relied on a document which is called an obligatory instruction, which was a kind of guideline requesting rigorous punishment for failure to carry out orders and for other criminal offences, and completely forgot about International Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, briefly, there was also a comment made about minority rights which, of course, you've covered in your report on page 14. But can you indicate whether or not the absence of explicitly discriminatory provisions is terribly significant in this type of order? I think you began to address it and were cut off.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this comes to the protection of minorities, it is not enough to talk about the equality of all citizens in general terms. The provisions such as we come across in the documents of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, in particular, in a document called "the Declaration of the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna," which addresses the equality of all, irrespective of their ethnicity or other elements, such provisions are lacking in the document -- similar documents of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. As for the equality, that is, the national equality of non-Croat citizens, there I must say that the acts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna cannot stand a serious test. If we juxtapose them with the then effective constitutional and legal acts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Croatia or Slovenia perhaps, then we can see that even in that domain, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna fell short of the criteria which were in effect in other republics emerging from the former Yugoslavia, which I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Ribicic. Just in response to a point raised on cross which you have addressed in your paper but should be brought to the further attention of the Court. It's already Exhibit 341.5A; it is on the district military courts. I would just ask you to indicate -- if the usher would be kind enough to put it on the ELMO. It would be looking at the first paragraph, which would be at the attachment you have, broj sest, strana tri, on the page that would end in 00860157. Can you indicate, please, what body appointed the judges. Who establishes the district military courts and who appoints the judges?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judges are elected and removed by the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and they made the solemn declaration before the president and other members of the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This is one of the places where there is no clear-cut distinction between the duties of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the president of the presidency of that Community. Because, in a manner of speaking, it is not logical to make one's solemn declaration before some other member of the presidency, as the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was a separate function. Evidently, there is inconsistency here, that this function is likened, or at least a sort of equality is drawn between the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the president of the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the same document, Article 20. Look at Article 20. It's fine if you can read it. As to the process of selection, please, where it says that the president --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The appointment of judges is by whom? The appointment of judges is by whom?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judges are appointed by the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna upon the nomination or proposal of a person heading the defence department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Ribicic, you addressed the issue of the assets of the JNA which were located in the municipalities of HZ HB but nonetheless on the territory of the sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you comment on what happened to those assets in terms of Bosnia receiving them; do you know? Was there a provision in these legislative enactments for Bosnia to receive any of the assets, or do they only go to one entity?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna took over those assets, there is not a word mentioning the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just so that the Court will have it, that is Z341.10, and the summary reflects what is the content. If we can just make it an exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, the human rights provisions that were discussed, including the statement that the current freedoms of the Muslims are owed to the Croat community, was September of 1993, as we were shown. Are you aware of a massacre that occurred in October 1993 in Vares called Stupni Do? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Give me one second to make sure I haven't missed anything, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issue of referendum was raised yesterday where the Defence indicated that some 90-something per cent of the Croat community voted at the referendum, and I would like to ask -- it is previously marked as Z48, if the usher could put it quickly on the ELMO, and I would be asking you to look at the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, you're coming to an end, I trust.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm trying to wind down. That's why I want to get as focused as I can quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've got until one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, it's not on the ELMO, but if you could just indicate, please, what the comments are -- it is a document signed by Mate Boban, and what is his comment about the European Community's assurances concerning the referendum, and what does he tell the Croat people to do?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 2, "Press Releases," we have Mate Boban's signature and that of the secretary of the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Ignac Kostroman, and it says: "So far, some communications to the president on behalf of the unauthorised persons has caused major perplexity among the Croat people as regards the official --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. There is a provision which discusses the representations of the European Community and the referendum. If could you find that, please. I'm afraid you have my copy, so I cannot direct you to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have either the text on the ELMO or ask the witness to speak slower, to read it slower.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it is the beginning of this press release, and this is what it says: "The assurances given by the European Community manifested in earlier discussions, as well as in yesterday's EC Conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina, indicate that the result of the forthcoming referendum would not prejudge the future constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This does not bring into question the fundamental principles of the conclusions of the HDZ BiH Main Board in Livno, which will still guard the sovereignty of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both within their ethnically established geographical areas and everywhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Yes. What this means is that the Croatian Democratic Union, prior to the referendum, wanted to make its official stand clear, and this official position was that the referendum would not prevent an autonomous organisation of the Croat people and its independence within the future Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, if I were to present to you sort of a little genealogy, would it be fair and correct to say that the HVO was born of the HZ HB which was born of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one analyses various normative acts, then one can glean that, especially from the original decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. As for other documents, that is, various testimonies, statements, or articles in the press, or meetings, the links that exist between the HDZ, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the HVO, or the link that exists between the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HDZ in the Republic of Croatia, can better be -- are more evident in those other documents; that is, the normative acts do not give us sufficient information to indicate that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna served the Republic of Croatia. However, this does transpire from other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is the answer no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps my question wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no, insofar as normative acts are concerned, and the answer is yes, insofar as all other documents are concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final point, if you are able to answer this, Dr. Ribicic, from some of the inferences drawn during cross. In the systems of the former Yugoslavia, indeed, in block countries, are you familiar with a concept called a political officer in the military? And if you are familiar, can you comment on the role of that political officer and the type of authority he or she might have?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different theories, different practices, and I'm not really conversant with the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ribicic, thank you for coming to the International Criminal Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now released and free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is one matter I want to deal with administratively when the witness has left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have another witness here, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have a total of three more witnesses this week; two are here and available this afternoon, each of them is short. They will not exhaust the available court sitting time for the week, and each of them can be available today -- well, two of them can be available today or tomorrow, at your convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I had in mind that we ought to deal, if possible, with the transcripts as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, would it be convenient to make a start with the transcripts after the adjournment and see how we get on with that? The witness can be here tomorrow, can he or she?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Both witnesses, I do believe, can be here tomorrow, and I don't believe either of them has any pressing personal concerns to get their evidence over with quickly. I better just check that with Mr. Lopez-Terres. He's been dealing with one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They've both been told they're likely to testify today, so to some extent, they've got themselves ready. But I don't think they fall into the category, for example, of the last witness, whose personal circumstances I might have pressed hard. I'm sure they can both be persuaded to come tomorrow. I know Mr. Lopez-Terres has difficulties tomorrow morning, but I'll get round those so that he's able to take the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long would one of the witnesses be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres considers his witness will be 40 minutes in chief, and there may be very limited cross-examination. It's a village witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's take that witness then, if she is ready, and then we will deal with the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's also the Defence Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exactly, so the earlier we start on that, the better. An encouragement, I hope, to the witness. Twenty-five to three. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m. 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are indeed Mr. Ismet Halilovic, born in 1955?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're an engineer at the Bratstvo factory in Novi Travnik, where you live?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You specialised in industrial machinery?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, in the course of October 1992, when the second conflict was ongoing in Novi Travnik, is it true that three soldiers belonging to the HVO forces came to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, you were living in the lower part of the town, known as Bare?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us, briefly, on the map that I am going to give you, the position of your building? This is Z1960, exhibit.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I think I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us where you were living at the time, that is, in October 1992, in the lower part of the town?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I lived here [indicates], and later in 1993 I left to this part of town, where I live now [indicates]. The street is called Kalinska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you've shown us already, let me repeat: You lived first in Bare, and then in January 1993 you moved to go to the upper part of the town, known as Kalinska.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those three soldiers which appeared at your place, they threatened you with weapons and said that they were looking for a sniper?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was their excuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you knew, were there one or several snipers in your building or in the part of town that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in that area there were no snipers at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already told us that you considered this to be an excuse, a pretext.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they came to your place, they uttered insults at your expense?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were customary insults of Muslims, using various curses. I don't know if it's necessary for me to repeat them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps that won't be useful. Then they searched your apartment, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the search, they found a 7.65 pistol, which you lawfully had in your possession for several years and for which you had a permit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two days later, after this visit, three other HVO soldiers, one of whom was in black uniform, the other two in camouflage uniform, all armed with guns, came again to your building?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was again during that conflict or, rather, the very next day. They came demanding that the Muslims or, rather, balijas, as they called us, who had garages in the building should come out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you obeyed, and you came out, together with other neighbours from the building, in front of your garage?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because a solder was standing next to my garage, asking whose garage it was, and I answered that it was mine. Then they demanded the keys. One of them took the car, and the other one went with me to take my driving licence. We went upstairs. He pointed the gun at me. I was looking for it, but I couldn't find it. And then they went downstairs and the three of them went off with my car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did one of the soldiers tell you which village he came from?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to see who he was. I said that he seemed familiar, and he said, "No, you can't know me, sir. I'm an Ustashe from Rankovici."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Rankovici is a village close to Novi Travnik, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, next to Novi Travnik, and it is part of Novi Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were informed, when your car was taken, that other Muslims were victims of the same kind of procedure by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, it was not just my car that was driven off but many others that they could get their hands on. They would take away not only cars but other objects that they considered to be important for them at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that one of your neighbours and two colleagues from work had their cars stolen in the same way.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was making my statement, I remembered that Mr. Mustafa Velatovac and Mr. Ratko Vujovic had told me that their cars were taken away in the same way, as well as Suljo Krnjic's, who also was a neighbour of mine. So his car was taken. Later on I learned of many other cases, but I just remembered these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just told us that your car and the cars of these people were taken away. Was it a theft or a requisitioning?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: In my view it was theft, because if it was to be used for military purposes, then as far as I know, some kind of document should have been provided so that later on I could claim it back. But as they gave us no certificates, no papers, I consider it to be theft, plain and simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after this theft, you met by chance, I think, Mr. Marinko Marelja, a local influential Croat in Travnik municipality and who owned the Grand cafe. You met him in front of this cafe. Could you tell us briefly the gist of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Marinko Marelja from before, because he was living in Novi Travnik. He was the owner of this Cafe Grand, which I used to visit frequently, and we knew each other. Passing by the Grand cafe, Mr. Marinko Marelja came by, and I said, rather in passing, whether he could help me trace my car, because I knew that he had influence over these people. I knew that he was a former policeman, and since we knew one another, I tried to regain possession of my car with his assistance. However, he answered, "Never mind your car, Cuna. Better move to Kalinska. Brothers are brothers, and it's better if they separate, and this town will be divided into the upper and lower part of Novi Travnik."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he told us [sic] that the town would be divided, he meant by the Croats of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As the Serbs had already left, he must have meant the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your vehicle was ultimately found by a cousin and you were able to regain possession of it, so we don't need to go into the details of that.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of days later, I managed to find my car, thanks to a relative of mine who recognised it, and I got my car back. Not thanks to the soldiers or anyone else but thanks to this relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your cousin took the car away from the person, the soldier, who was driving it by force?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't call it by force, but he's a big man. This was in Travnik, they were outside their own territory, and as they didn't have the documents for the car, he considered this to be theft too, and so they gave up the car quite easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of December 1992 and January 1993, the Muslims living in the same area as you were given ultimatums to have to abandon this district by phone calls or by HVO soldiers who appeared at their apartments.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were many such instances in December and January. Many people were intimidated. Soldiers would come with socks over their heads, so I don't know who they were, and they were inflicting terror on the people to force the people out, again giving the reason that this would be a Croatian town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these visits or phone calls, threats were uttered, death threats.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that there were death threats, but there were words to the effect, "You must leave within 24 hours or you'll see what will happen to you," and words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself didn't receive any such threats, but you took the threats received by others very seriously.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many realised this and left before me. Unfortunately, I didn't immediately. But this could be felt in the air, as our people are prone to say, that we needed to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the persons who were threatened was one of your colleagues from work.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dzenana Bubric, I said that, and I recalled just then her name. But there were others, and I can't remember exactly all the names of those people, but many left under threat. I cannot say that I did so because I was not threatened, but if I may, I should like to explain why I decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do that.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I had a large number of colleagues at work who were Croats, and when this person came up to me, with whom I eventually exchanged apartments, to ask me if I wanted to exchange with him, I was still hesitant; however, I asked another colleague of mine, who is younger than me and whom I had helped a great deal at work and I thought I could count on his sincerity, his name was Mr. Blazen Kovac, and I asked him, "Blazen, please tell me, what is the situation, and should I really exchange apartments and move to the upper part of town?" His answer was, "Cuna, judging by what I have heard and what I do know, you would be better off if you left." He didn't tell me specifically what he had heard, but he simply informed me in this way that I should leave, and that is what I did. I went to the upper part of town at the end of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while later, on the Sunday, the 7th of February, 1993, you decided to take back some bags to a former neighbour and to collect some things from your former garage.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I moved on the 31st of January, and seven days later, that is, the 7th of February, with my daughter and two sons of my brother's, I collected bags which I had borrowed from my former neighbours when moving. I wanted to give those bags back, and I thought at the same time I could collect a few small belongings from my garage. This happened on the 7th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: January. I'm sorry. The witness said "January".

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation];.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the Petar Mecava Street on your way?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I gave the bags back and I dropped in at my neighbour's, Pocrnjak, I had a cup of coffee with him, and I took a small wheelbarrow, intending to transport those things to the new apartment. In the meantime, my brother came, and since he had a garage too and he wanted to take some things out too, we took a trailer and we loaded some stuff on that trailer and headed off towards the upper part of town. In the Petar Mecava Street, we were intercepted by three HVO soldiers who asked us, first of all, "Where are you going?" Without any second thought, I said, "We're going to Kalinska, we're taking some things with us." "And what are your names?" When we gave them our names, Ismet and Izet, the swearing started, they cursed our balija mothers. "What have you been waiting for? Why didn't you leave earlier on?" and then he cocked his automatic rifle and put the barrel in my mouth. I still wasn't aware of the situation that my brother, the children, and I were in, but in view of the presence of the children, I thought surely they couldn't do something bad to us, and this was daytime, about 1.30 in the afternoon. After all, it's daytime, it's in the centre of town. He cocked his gun and said, "You can see it's loaded," and he said, "Unload those things from the trailer so we can see what's in there." So I started taking things down, and he then said, "Hurry up. Hurry up," And he found a small axe, and he asked, "What's this?" and I said, "It's a small axe." He waved with it, turning the blunt side to hit me with it, and he hit me in the chest. I sort of stumbled, and when he saw I was still on my feet, since the axe fell out of his hand as he did this, he turned his gun around and hit me here [indicates], between the eyebrows, and you can still see the scar. I fell on my knees, I was covered in blood, and I simply asked him, "Young man, why are you doing this?" and without any hesitation, from a distance of about three metres, he shot at me, and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us where you were shot?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: It was a bullet which hit me -- the entry wound was in the neck, and here [indicates]. The exit wound was on the front side of my neck. The exit wound is slightly larger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you lost consciousness as a result.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I lost consciousness, and then when I came to, I somehow managed to stand up, with blood all over me. I didn't know where I was, what had happened. At that moment, two HVO policemen, because they were not far away -- some 20 metres also was a police station, behind that building -- they gave me signs to hurry up and to come close to them. I approached them and I went into their premises asking for help, thinking to give me something at least to bandage my wound, but the answer they gave me was that they had no bandages. Then I asked them to give me a lift to the emergency aid, and they said they had no petrol, so that I had to come out into the street again. At that moment, a Golf was passing by, and I stopped in the middle of the street, and I guess people, when saw me all bloody, they stopped, picked me up, and took me to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether the soldier, the one who pointed his rifle at you and shot, did he have any particular insignia, any badges?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That fellow that fired at me, I learned his name. His name was Ivica Mlakic. He had the letter "U" on his cap, and he never even hesitated to mention that he belonged to the Ustashe. I think he was very proud of the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- your impression was that those soldiers or some other soldiers were there drunk or perhaps slightly intoxicated?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say whether somebody's drunk. I mean, if he can pick up first a small axe, then the rifle, and quite consciously ill-treat somebody, I don't know. Of course, I didn't give them a breathing test, so I don't know, but I really --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that one of the soldiers, before that shot was fired, that he tried to intervene?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I [sic] tried. He was a fair-haired hair [sic], and he was Josip Marko. He was the son of the father who worked nearby, and he tried to stop this Mlakic, to stop him from ill-treating us, but he simply pushed him away and would not let him stop him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since he lost consciousness, you could not see what happened to your brother, to Izet, but you received information about the circumstances of his death from their own children, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that from the children and many other people who knew me. And very many other people in Travnik knew me; they told me later on what had happened. But the children, of course, were on the spot. At the moment when he fired at me and I fell in the street, and my brother also thought that I had been killed, and they must have thought that too, that I was dead. And he then simply cried out, "You've killed my brother." I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: And at that moment that man fired at him too, in his stomach, and when he saw that he was still alive, he came close to him and fired another bullet in his forehead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother Izet was 40 when that happened, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was born in 1953.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had three children and worked for a humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had three children. Yes. At that time he worked for Merhamet, and apart from Merhamet he was also active in the Red Cross in the municipality. It was set up to help people with food and other humanitarian relief, and he was active in that because he was not a soldier. Both of us were in civilian clothes. Throughout that period of time I was under work obligation, so I wasn't taking any military part in anything as a soldier, nor did my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already addressed that subject, Mr. Halilovic. While you were in hospital, other HVO soldiers, who were guarded by Susa, who was in the same hospital, and you were asked to reveal the identity of these soldiers, of these three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in the hospital after a traffic accident, he was there too. I believe he was a H-O-S commander, a HOS commander. He was called Susa, and he was in the hospital unconscious, and there were always four or five of his men there guarding him. Those fellows also came from somewhere around Novi Travnik, from Rankovici, Bucici. And they had heard about the case, about the incident, and they came to me and they gave me the names of those people, of the people who had done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those three soldiers, Mlakic, Milanovic, and Miletic, they, according to what you were told, came from the village of Rankovici, did they?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know if they belonged to the Novi Travnik HVO Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I learnt that Ivica Kambic was their commander, and I knew him well, because he also lived in the village of Novi Travnik. So they belonged to that Novi Travnik unit of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to show you three documents, which are all medical documents. Mr. Halilovic, do you recognise these documents? Were they documents which were issued you at that time, on the 3rd of March, 1993, at the time of your hospitalisation? This is Z520.1, 520.2, and 604.2.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The document Z604.2 is the document that I was admitted to the hospital, rather, the discharge document which says what are the findings and where I had received wounds. The second document was issued by a neuropsychiatrist, and it shows that vertebra 1 was injured, and that I also -- and that -- and there was a numbness of my neck and in the back of my head and in the shoulder. And the third document, 604.1, is the document that I was issued --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. We shall come to that. We shall come to that. We have not yet come to that particular document. Yes, you have it before you, but we have not come to it yet. Are you still suffering the effects of these wounds?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. My left arm is still numb. I feel this numbness in my neck and my head. And because my vertebra was damaged, of course I feel that. Needless to say, whenever the weather changes, I am in severe pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The end of February 1993, you were called by a judge called Percinlic, who was a judge with the military court in Travnik, an HVO judge?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made a statement. You made a statement about how you had been victimised. You made a statement before the judge.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was summoned to the military court in Travnik. Zeljko Percinlic was the judge there, and I made a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later in April 1993, you were issued with a document from that particular military court, and saying that against Josip Milanovic, against whom the investigation was conducted, he had been detained.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was this, Z604.1, whereby I was informed that an investigation has been launched against Josip -- against Ivica Mlakic. However, I was not satisfied with this, because the other two were exempt from any criminal investigation. So I called the Prosecutor and said that I would file an appeal. However, I had no opportunity to do so, because shortly after that the conflict broke out in Travnik between the armija and the HVO, so that it has remained unresolved to this day and nobody was called to account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, the name of Ivica -- the person called Ivica Mlakic still lives in the locality of Rankovici, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And somewhat later, but in 1993, that is, in October or November 1993, the building in which you lived at the time was hit by a shell, and it caused several -- some -- the death of about a dozen civilians?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had just come back from work. I was having lunch, and I was in the kitchen, and that is in the front part of the building, when I felt a very powerful detonation. At that same moment, I went out to the back part where my bedroom was, and I saw smoke and I heard screams of people. At that moment, I could not see any people downstairs because of this thick smoke, but I went downstairs because this shell had hit the flat of my brother's wife. I just went down to see how had the children and she fared and whether there were any injured there. And then people went down to carry away the wounded. I believe that some 10 or maybe 11 people were killed on that occasion. While I was cleaning the flat, my brother's flat, I found a shrapnel of the shell and I saw "128" written on it. To my knowledge, because I work in the military industry, it was a shrapnel of a 128-millimetre shell. I think, that is, it is my opinion, but not only my opinion, that that shell had been fired by the HVO, because if you look how -- where the building faces and where the shell came from, I believe it was the HVO. I do not know if anybody went out to find the facts. This is only my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You believe that the shell could have been fired from the direction of Rankovici?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because it could have only come from that direction. That is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any military facilities near your building?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Croat families living in that area or in that building?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, during the same period of time, you could see that the snipers were regularly firing at the civilian population, and you could see that as you went to work and back from work daily?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because I was under a labour obligation, I would leave my flat to go to the factory every morning, and we would take a shortcut through the wood. But there were quite a number of places where we had to run across because the snipers never stopped firing from the location of Relay, of the transmitter, which is on a hill immediately above the fire brigade station above Novi Travnik, where the transmitter used to be before. That's why we call it that. And throughout the conflict, snipers fired at us and other civilians, and those of us who went to comply with the labour obligations and other civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that at least three persons died as a result of these sniper shots.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already mentioned. Many more people -- there were many more casualties and lethalities [sic].
