I knew Redzib Sivro, because I knew him well, and Nazif Kopcic, because I knew him. They were all people who worked for Bratstvo. And I also knew my friend's wife who was killed in her flat, because the bullet simply went through the glass, hit her, and killed her there and then. Those are people whose names I remember at the moment, but there were quite a number of both -- of people who were wounded and killed, all from those positions held at Relay, at the former transmitter station site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, allow me to introduce myself. I'm Mitko Naumovski, a lawyer from Zagreb, and I'm one of the counsel for the accused Kordic. I'll ask you a few questions, but I must say something before I begin. Because we speak the same language and we can understand one another as soon as we have uttered a thought, will you please pause a little after you've heard my question so as to give time to the interpreters to interpret my questions. I believe my questions will not take long. The first very short subject is the first day of the conflict in October 1992, when three soldiers, as you say, came and searched your apartment. When they came, they asked you if you had any weapons, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. They asked me if I had a sniper weapon or a rifle. They came using as an excuse that a sniper was firing from that building, so they were looking for a sniper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I will jog your memory if I tell you what you told the investigators in November 1998. First page, third paragraph: "The soldiers asked me if I had any weapons, and I said no," and then you added, as an afterthought, what weapons you had in mind, but a sniper weapon is not mentioned anywhere. You mentioned a sniper weapon today for the first time.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not think that anybody should seize a pistol for which I had a license. It is a pistol 7.65. I had a permit for it. And the statement which I gave them, that is what I said: They came and said as a pretext that a sniper was firing from that building, and I said I did not have any weapon of that type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. That was my introductory question, if I may call it that. Let us now move on to the second incident when your car was seized. You already described the car and how it was taken away from you; there is no need to go back to it, but we agree that the car was given back to you, don't we?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of questions that have to do with residents in the Novi Travnik municipality. Can we agree, Mr. Halilovic, that as early as September 1992, in particular, some 4,000 or 5,000 Muslims arrived in Novi Travnik, driven away by Serbs from the areas that they had taken?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes; that is, I don't know how many of them, but they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should say it was a few thousand of them.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not think they were that many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But we agree that they came to Novi Travnik. A certain number, never mind how many of them, came to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and they mostly were accommodated in villages, in private houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree also that some of those people who were not accommodated in villages were bringing major pressure to bear on the inhabitants of the upper part of town to move out of their flats? And by this, I mean, in the first place, the Kalinska Street.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: What inhabitants do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Croats, in this case.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any such case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you exchanged a flat with a Croat who used to live on that very street, on Kalinska Street.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Croat suggested to you to exchange flats, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to give me an answer because of the record.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but may I explain it slowly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we agree that your colleague at work, this Croat, asked you to exchange flats? He must have had reason for that.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he must have been better informed than I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you know anything more specific about reasons for which he wanted to exchange flats? Did any of the Croats with whom you worked, they must have told you that they were suffering some unpleasantness in that part of the town -- well, that same gentleman.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: That same gentleman, Mladen Dujmuscic, he worked with me, and he never -- and that can be ascertained because I live in his flat now -- never, he never -- throughout that period, nobody attacked him or said a bad word to him. The then commander, Refik Lendo, and I can give you the name of a man that I know, and that is Mr. Boro Miletic, his wife is a Croat, and he told him when he -- when Boro asked him, he replied, "Boro, as for departure, you can stay here, and I'll even give you a soldier to take care of you." So there was no coercion by anyone, at least not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that Boro Miletic, he wasn't a Croat, was he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: His wife was a Croat and he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But perhaps you know those people, I might give you those names, I mean, people who suffered various things in Kalinska. For instance, a lawyer, Ivan Grubesic, was attacked there. You must have heard of him because he was not a known figure in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Marka Savkovic, and so forth, Danilo Lukovic; there are quite a number of people who were told by TO members to move out, something similar to what you say happened in the lower part of town.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Mr. Grubesic, but to be quite honest, I don't know if he went through anything like that. And as for Mladen Dujmuscic, I'm positive that he never experienced anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do we agree that he asked you to exchange flats and that you agreed in the end and that you did, in fact, exchange your flat for his, to wind this story up.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did ask me, because our flat was the same size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're not interested in those details. They're not important anymore. Thank you. You mentioned a moment ago the talk with Marelja and said something to the following effect. You said: "Well, even brothers get divided up, so we can split up too in this town and live in two parts," and from this I can conclude that if there are two parts, one would be the Croatian sector and the other would be the Muslim sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what Mr. Marelja had in mind; I just know what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question to you in a different way. Tell us, please, what the situation was like before the signing of the Washington Agreement. Was the town divided? We don't have to speak about actual borders and where it was divided. I'm talking about 1994.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We agree then. Thank you. I have several questions to ask you with regard to what happened to you on the 7th of February, but I'll be brief. If I understood you correctly, the person who shot at you and your brother was Ivica Mlakic, Marijan's son from Rankovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give us a clear answer so that the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ivica Mlakic was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not want to attach greater importance to that detail than it deserves, but when you spoke a moment ago, you said that you couldn't see whether the soldiers were drunk or not. That was a question put to you by the Prosecutor. Is that right? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what people mean by "drunk".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you what you told the investigators. You said that the soldiers appeared to be drunk.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably appeared to be drunk, if I said that, but whether they were actually drunk, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But you agree that you made that statement. I don't want to insist upon the degree or details. Today you spoke about the court proceedings that took place later on, and from the documents that I have come by, I find that at the end of February 1993, you were interviewed by this same judge, Percinlic, in February 1993, that was.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the statement that you gave on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not. It is with Mr. Percinlic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were interrogated as the plaintiff, you knew the crime that had been committed and who the proceedings were started against.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender two documents into evidence, and they can be assigned the same number with points 1 and 2, if you agree, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, it is important for you to look at the Croatian version of the text. So underneath the English text, you have the Croatian, the document you're now holding in your left hand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered D187/1 and D188/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, as I say, you have the Croatian version at the back. Look at page 1, please; that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a request for an investigation to be conducted, and it was a request made by the district prosecutor in Travnik. With regard to this request, Mr. Halilovic was interviewed as a witness and as the plaintiff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this document, Mr. Halilovic, it would emerge that the proceedings were taken against the first suspect, Ivica Mlakic, and Josip Milanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The proceedings were initiated but never brought to a close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After the investigation was completed, and that was according to the law of the former Yugoslavia, you were sent this document; it is document Z604.1, and from this document, we see that the judge is informing you, against one of these individuals, that is to say, Milanovic, that he stopped all further investigation, and that Ivica Mlakic was accused of the crime he committed. The final sentence is instruction to you as the plaintiff, telling you that you have the right to ask for an additional investigation or to file a charge against Josip Milanovic for that same criminal act, and you are given a deadline provided for by law, and the deadline was eight days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but I was never able to take them up on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had the chance of bringing charges against Milanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at the other document, please, the one on your right-hand side. The original is in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other document, Your Honours, is an indictment of the military courts in Travnik, which is sent to the district court in Travnik, against Ivica Mlakic for committing the crime at the expense of Mr. Halilovic and his late brother. In the former Yugoslavia, this was qualified as an attempt to kill a number of individuals. One individual was, in fact, killed, whereas the other one received serious bodily injury, so this was an attempt -- an act of killing attempted by several individuals, and Ivica Mlakic was accused of that crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at page 1 of the document, and it was precisely with respect to the act that was committed as you described it.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, in your statement to the investigators, you said that nobody was taken into custody because of the crime that had been committed, and I can read that portion of the statement to you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I had reasons for saying that, because that same Mr. Mlakic, who killed my brother and wounded me, ten days later was seen in the lower part of town. That was the piece of information that I received, and the information was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see him personally, did you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't recognise him even to this day, because I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why am I saying this to you? I'm saying this because ten days later he could not be on the road, because from this indictment, and please read the first paragraph on page 1, you have basic data about the individual, and it states that he was in custody from the 7th of February, 1993, whereas the indictment was written later on. Do you agree that he was in prison at the time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I agree with you, but I told Mr. Jurcevic the same thing, because he also said that this individual was in prison, whereas I was able to tell him that he was not actually in prison but was located in the lower part of town somewhere, and that is something that I know for a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't see him personally, did you? You heard this from someone else. It was what we like to call rumours, or hearsay.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see him, and I couldn't see him, because I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one more question, perhaps, and I apologise, but could you just tell me one detail with regard to the indictment, that you were interviewed as a witness in this proceedings, and that is contained on page 3 of the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have two questions, brief ones. Do you agree with me that the Serbs, and I'm thinking of the army, the Serbian soldiers, that they shelled Novi Travnik from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did shell it on two occasions, and they shelled the Bratstvo factory twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did anybody else shell it, apart from the air?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about the shell that hit your house, and you said that you were able to ascertain its calibre. Do you have any knowledge of weaponry, in view of the fact that you worked at the Bratstvo plant? Was it a VBR calibre?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was a VBR or a light rocket-launcher, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Today you said -- that is to say, I understood you to have made a conclusion that the shell had come from the direction and positions held by the HVO, but I can conclude from that that you don't actually -- you're not actually sure where the shell came from, which direction, if it was this VBR-type shell.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am quite certain of the direction it came from, but of course I cannot claim that. There are experts who can do that for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one further question. You talked about snipers.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the high-rise in the town is, where the 9th and 10th floors were burnt, one of those three sky-rise buildings that exist in town?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are four of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, there are four, but one of them had two of its top floors burnt?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: One had been burnt down completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's the one. Do you agree that some time after October 1992, it was from this particular high-rise that the snipers attacked Croats in town?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say. I was not a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is impossible that you never heard about any cases of Croats being hit by snipers in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've been living in Novi Travnik for 45 years, and I only visited the lower part of town once after the events that took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you want to tell me is that you have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I want to say that I have no contact whatsoever with the lower part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours, for your patience. I have completed my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't have any questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question to the witness, if I may, just one. Re-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, the two documents shown to you today were Exhibits D1181 and D1187/1, coming from the military court in Travnik. Did you ever have that document in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were, indeed, the victim in these proceedings instituted.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had no knowledge of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see those documents at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they public documents or part of the judicial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot straightaway say whether this is correct or what this is. I just said, on the basis of what I see, I cannot tell you immediately, in one minute, whether this is what you say it is. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to pronounce yourself on the authenticity of this document, I'm just asking whether other persons have the access to these documents, excepting those involved.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I was never shown this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the accused Dario Kordic may have gained possession of this document when it had nothing to do with him?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I tried to get hold of such documents from the military court of the HVO, because I have a friend working in court, but there were no documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw the indictment today and the requests for the institution of an investigation into the event. Do you know whether there was a condemnation of Ivica Mlakic for murder and attempted murder? Was he convicted?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HALILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, and that is what I told Mr. Naumovski, that that young man, Ivica Mlakic, was free ten days later. As far as I know and the information I have, he was never indicted. He was never charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, and I wish you every success in your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a matter of some concern to us, particularly Mr. Lopez-Terres, who is familiar with the judicial system, how these documents come from what should apparently be a judicial system, not available to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt some inquiries can be made or something. Mr. Nice, it's 10 to 4. I don't think there's going to be time to deal with much in the way of transcripts. It seems sensible to deal with the pre-Defence conference today. We've got two witnesses left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't think it will be a problem dealing with them and all the administrative matters this week. Perhaps if the first witness can be taken tomorrow morning. He's very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then we can perhaps turn to administrative matters thereafter. There's one matter I've got to report on. It probably should be in a very short private session, if we could have that. I'm asked to make -- report by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, so I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I propose to deal with the pre-Defence conference now, unless there are any other matters to be dealt with immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There may be one or matter I want to raise at the end, and there is one topic I want to be heard on in relation to the pre-Defence conference, but I'll wait my turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Turning to Rule 73 ter in its original form, which we've been operating under as far as this case is concerned, the Rule requires us, prior to the commencement by the defence of its case to hold, or we may hold, rather, a conference in which to order to Defence, before the commencement of its case but after the close of the case for the prosecution, to file the following: admissions and a statement of other matters which aren't in dispute; a statement of contested matters of fact and law; a list of witnesses the Defence intends to call, with the name and pseudonym of each, a summary of the facts on which each will testify, the points in the indictment as to which each will testify, and the estimated length of time required for each; a list of exhibits Defence intends to offer, stating, where possible, whether the Prosecutor has any objection as to authenticity. Now, the position is this: The Defence is due to begin its case, at the moment, on the 10th of April. Clearly, these matters should be in hand before then. I can't remember offhand what the final date we decided on for the Prosecution to produce all its witnesses was, but I think it was three weeks before the trial. There have been several since.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Five weeks, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I believe the last day for the Prosecution's case is 10 March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about at what stage before the Prosecution put its case on it was obliged to produce its witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Actually, may it please the Court. I anticipated we might be discussing that and seeking some parity. Your Honours' scheduling order of 22 March 1999 lays that all out, and if you don't have it at the ready, I can supply it to you. I believe, pursuant to that scheduling order, and I seek some parity with it, the Prosecution was obligated, six days before the start of our case on April 12th, to supply us with one-half of their witness summaries and the remaining summaries 15 days after that, by April 27. And the Prosecution was obligated, 12 days before the start of the case on April 12th, to supply the Defence with a list of witnesses for the first six weeks of trial, that date being March 31, 1999. Then, of course, we have a rolling, two-week list of witnesses. Along those lines, if it may please the Court, and given the parameters of the Court's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pausing there. You say "parity." They were obliged to produce the material, the supporting material for the indictment at an earlier stage. So they had made some disclosure before any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's true, but it rubs salt into the wounds with respect to that issue, sir. The supporting material for the indictment and the ultimate material that we're trying are two different sets of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear what your proposals are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What I propose, Your Honour, is that assuming the evidence closes on the 10th of March, our motion for judgement of acquittal would be due on March 17. I would propose first that even should the Prosecution end its case a day or two or even a week earlier, that date be a firm date, March 17, for the filing of our motion for judgement of acquittal. I seek that because it gives us some certainty to plan our work and to allocate tasks. I would propose that the Prosecution be given until March 24, 7 days, to reply to our motion for judgement of acquittal. Argument has been scheduled for March 30. That would give all of us time to consume the Prosecution's answer and study the various documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, pausing there. I know what your application is, but if the Prosecution were to finish earlier, I think the Rules would oblige you to produce your motion within a week. I'll be reminded if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I think it's Rule 98, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May I ask this, then. This is a slight bend, and I acknowledge that. We could, of course, file a one or two-page pro forma motion for judgement of acquittal, followed up by really the meat of what we intend to say in our brief. So should the Prosecution close its case, say, March 1, we certainly can file a pro forma motion for judgement of acquittal within the time contemplated by the Rule, but we would ask for leave and an extension to file our full set of papers by March 17, if not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll certainly consider that. What we're looking for, speaking for myself, is not a detailed brief; it is a skeleton which sets out the argument and, where need be, the references, so we can follow the argument. That's the important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'll carry that back to the brief writer and writers and make that known. We propose further that that document will fairly and articulately set out contested issues of law and fact and, consequently, I think moot out any need under 73(A) to more fully set those matters out. We therefore would ask the Court that on March 30, we supply the Prosecution with our witness list and our exhibit list; and on April 4, supply the Prosecution with the witness summaries for the first six weeks of trial; and by April 25, the second half of that list. And these are approximately the same time, given the weekends and disparities in the calendar, that the Prosecution gave the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At some stage, the Trial Chamber will want to go through these witnesses to decide how many really need be called and how many can be dealt with in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, again, just thinking ahead, the motion for judgement of acquittal we put great weight on and great faith, and your decision in that regard, presumptively being made before we start our case, will chart everyone's course in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You say that you will provide the witness list and the exhibit list on the 30th of March. On the 4th of April the witness summaries for the first six weeks; the 25th of April, second half of list. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What I meant, actually, Judge, is we would divide the summaries. The first half of the witness list would be summarised and then the next half summarised thereafter on April 25. And that first half wouldn't be just alphabetical; it will be the people who will be testifying in the first six weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So by the 25th of April, you would have completed everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we'll know what it is, the scope of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, anything you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a lot. As to equality of means or arms, it has to be borne in mind -- there should be borne in mind, first, that the resources of the parties are worth having in mind. We now know the degree of assistance supplied to the Defence by the State of Croatia and by the Croatian part of the republic. We know a lot else about their resources. They have very considerable resources indeed. We have some resources but, of course, we have duties, both in relation to our relations to the parties who assist us and also in relation to the position of adverse material; that is to say, favourable material to the other side. Second, we have provided, years ago, the vast majority of the material in the original confirming material. A great deal of material was provided thereafter, and it's not just summaries; it's full statements. Exhibits were provided along the way, some, more, of course, later, and then all statements, apart from those that were provided in respect of late-noticed witnesses, were provided before trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Some people would say you're lucky to be getting these statements. It's not a provision which some of us are used to, the Prosecution get the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I respectfully say that would be to instinctively incorporate into these proceedings what may apply elsewhere but doesn't apply here, where there is supposed to be equality of arms or means. So that the position is that the Defence start off in a vastly favourable position and that the Court should attempt to redress that in balance to some degree by making strict orders at this juncture. What sort of summaries should be provided? We apparently won't be provided with witness statements. This is a case where there's been no voluntary disclosure of any kind. In our respectful submission, the decision in -- yes. There's a Mostar case where decisions have already been made that the summaries to be served, as I am informed -- I haven't yet seen the order -- are to be as least as detailed as the sorts of summaries that we've been providing, and that, in our respectful submission, is what should be provided, and at this stage. There is no reason not to. There is every reason why that should be done, and even then the position will not remotely match that which is provided by the Prosecution. The Chamber will know that I have been making this point for some time, and that I made the point with reinforced emphasis when the degree of assistance available to the Defence became known. Further, provision of summaries in that degree of detail will both enable the Chamber to exercise its discretion or judgement in relation to the number of witnesses to be called, and will, I hope, enable me to decide which witnesses it isn't necessary to trouble attending at court, for unlike the Defence, I will have absolutely no hesitation in allowing statements or summaries to be placed before the Chamber uncontested where there is no contest. Not, of course, something that's been an approach by the Defence, to my considerable concern. But there is every reason, within these Rules, both the present Rules and, I suppose, the amended Rules insofar as they reflect the spirit of the institution, there is every reason for 73(B) order to be to the effect that before the commencement of its case, there should be filed a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify. No grounds for it being postponed until some date after the start of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, we have been, with the Prosecution, understanding to this extent: that you have frequently made the point that it is difficult for you to predict precisely which witnesses you can have. Orders were made at the very beginning of the case requiring witnesses to be notified by -- I forget what the last day was, but I think perhaps the 25th of May. I will be reminded. We have been dealing with applications in January and February of this year and, therefore, I think that the same sort of understanding, and I put it that way, neutrally, must be applied to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't disagree. But, again, the Chamber mustn't confuse one issue with the other. Applications you've been dealing with in respect of late-noticed witnesses is different entirely from the position about witnesses of whom the Defence already are aware and whom they already intend to call. It also has to be borne in mind that the whole business of preparing Defence witnesses is different from preparing Prosecution, to a significant extent. We have to prepare cases, or the investigators have to prepare cases or topics, and the witnesses are the subjects of statements that are taken; then there's a collection of witnesses identified for a particular case and so on, the material is served, the witness list is prepared, and so on. First the summary, then the fuller summary. The Defence are, of course, to a significant extent, bound to be being responsive to what's been served and what the Prosecution case is. So when they see a witness, they will be seeing a witness in relation to this case and no doubt taking a witness statement that relates to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, each one has his own style, but now you're engaging in explanations of the past. Couldn't you concentrate on the points proposed by the Defence, and very briefly so, because this is not the time to engage in a debate on the equality of arms, et cetera, on the way in which things were conducted, the differences between the Prosecution and the Defence, things that we know. We are here, we are professional Judges, and we don't need for you to explain to us the differences between the Prosecution and the Defence. After all, we have to concentrate on the points which will take us forward. There's a timetable that has been suggested, some very precise points. If you're not in agreement, tell us; if you agree, that's fine. So let's try and move on, please, without too much discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was dealing, first of all, with the Presiding Judge's concern about matters of history, and, indeed, I had been looking forward, and I still am, and I make the point, that for this case to be properly and fully litigated, the earlier notice I receive, or we receive, by way of full summaries of the Defence witness statements, the better; the better for efficiency, the better for the prospects of relieving witnesses the duty of attending, and, frankly, the more in line with the equality of means which the Judges of this Court have plainly intended to operate by the broadly parallel provisions of the two parts of Rule 73. That's the reason I referred to it, because it affects the position and answers the point the Presiding Judge was concerned about at the beginning. So we would invite you to say, first of all, that there should be no particular concession in relation to the service of any motion to acquit, and I can say no more than has already fallen from the lips of the Presiding Judge. I've made the point about the summary of the facts and, no doubt, Mr. Lopez-Terres, who's been trying to track down the precise terms of the order, will be able to deal with that, if not by today, by tomorrow. But we couldn't find the relevant people today or, indeed, yesterday, but it should be at least as full as our summaries, and they should, in our respectful submission, all be provided before the time when the case starts. In that way, we will be able to deal with the first witness and subsequent witnesses properly and fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stein, the point about the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have had experience in this Tribunal of summaries which are worthless, not in this case, but three lines. Entirely useless. Now, I had not understood that you would have engaged or, I might say, Mr. Kovacic, in that sort of activity. You would provide proper summaries of what it is the witness is going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me be clear, because the word "summary," "summary," and "summary" seems to be used in different contexts, and I must trace back to where we started, I'm afraid. The Prosecution's original summaries were just as you described, three lines. The Court instructed the Prosecution to amplify on those summaries, and they were amplified to a paragraph or more. We now have, as part of our experiment, daily summaries, complete -- 40, 50 paragraphs; six, seven pages -- given to us, as we've pointed out, regularly, an hour or, at best, an evening before the witness arrives. It is my intent that when we file our summaries with the Court, for them to be a page or less, so the Court knows what the witness is going to say, to what part of the indictment his testimony is focused, and the other requirements of 73. Not a book; one page or less. That is different from the experiment we have used consistently in this case, and we will, when the witness comes to The Hague, as the Prosecution has, talk to the witness in our final session with the witness, detail the specific paragraphs and points that he or she will testify, and serve up, within the time period allotted between the Victims and Witnesses Unit getting the witness to The Hague and his or her appearance in court, as the Prosecution has, a more detailed "summary". It's really not a summary; it's really an offer of proof, if you will, and that's the process we intend to use. So the Court will certainly have a roadmap into what our case is, the Prosecution will have the same roadmap that it gave us, and we will, in turn, when the witness is actually here in The Hague, be able to give far more than a roadmap; it will be a detailed account, and the Court can or the Prosecution can direct us and the witness to focus on paragraphs 1 through 6, as we have throughout the trial. If the Prosecution concedes paragraphs 7 through 12, there will be no questions, or perfunctory questions, and we will proceed as we have throughout these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may speak Croatian, it will be a little bit easier for me. [Interpretation] First of all, my learned friend from the Prosecution made a comparison of the resources available to the Defence. I don't know exactly what he refers to, and I find it rather confusing, because the Chamber has, in accordance with an earlier decision, filings from the Defence naming the members of the Cerkez Defence team, and I think there is no need for me to tell the Prosecution how strong or weak I am, because the Court has the necessary information. In any event, we're a very modest Defence team, as you know, and these deadlines that the Kordic Defence has mentioned is something that I'm unable to meet, I simply cannot, primarily because the Prosecution -- and I think -- I'd like to be wrong, but I think it did so for tactical reasons - that as of mid-December last year to the present, and this is obviously continuing, it has literally buried us with documents. So actually we have suspended the other activities in preparation of the defence which we had started when we saw what the Prosecution case was, but we have had to suspend those activities. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a point, in fact, here. Who is going to go first? Is the Kordic Defence going to go first and then finish, and then is the Cerkez Defence going to go? That is a fair point. Mr. Kordic is first on the indictment, isn't he, so in the normal course of events, he would go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, and we contemplate going first, to be quite candid, although I did facetiously flip a coin and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, in fact, just thinking aloud about this, if you are ready for, say, the first six weeks or so, that would give the Cerkez Defence longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, you will recall, Your Honour, I actually asked for more time as well, but we will comply with Your Honour's order and be ready on April 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, whatever day it is. But, on the other hand, Mr. Kovacic, you've got to comply with the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I shall try and convey our understanding of the Rules. Regarding this subject that you have just raised, who comes first, I must tell you that I was just going to ask you for some guidelines as to how we will organise things technically, because it would appear there is no standard in this Tribunal, when we have several accused and several Defenses, and I think theoretically we can go successively or in parallel. If you give us some instructions in that regard, that would, of course, be helpful for us. Because if we're talking about two separate defenses, then the Kordic case should begin within the time limits you have set, they will complete their case, and then I will begin. Of course, this could be treated differently too. We did discuss this question amongst ourselves, the two Defence teams, and it seems to me -- actually, we still haven't definitely defined it because we don't know what the position of Your Honours is. But if I can put it bluntly, regarding the general allegations, the background, the environment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you just wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we've been considering the position, and we think broadly what should happen is that the Kordic Defence should put its case on first and complete it before the Cerkez Defence starts, that's in terms of orderliness. But it may be that during the course of that order, things will change. I have in mind avoiding duplication of evidence, and I hope that you are combining with counsel for Mr. Kordic as far as possible to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's why, frankly, Your Honour, it would be immensely helpful if the Cerkez Defence, at least on a preliminary level, files its witness list, expected documents, at the same time we do, preliminarily, their defence going on substantially after ours, so that we can actually look at each others' -- we will certainly be meeting before then -- and cross off and eliminate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, you heard what Mr. Stein says. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, that sounds well from the standpoint of practicality, but I'm not sure that I will be able to respect the time limits. But if I may add, Your Honour, to be the second Defence has its advantages and disadvantages. In this case, if we are going to go successively, as you have indicated, this alternative, then it is certainly not in our interest, and I can promise you that, that we have no interest in repeating the evidence, because I believe that we all accept the old maxim of criminal law, beneficio cohesiones, if I may caricature things. If the Kordic Defence brings some good evidence, which I consider to be relevant for me, rest assured that I will not repeat that same evidence, and of course in my argument, I will refer to that evidence, and surely I have that right. I don't think that there can be any doubt that if the Cerkez Defence does the same thing, then this applies both ways; there's no dilemma about it. But if I may go back to my main point. We know more now, and that is that this Chamber is at least opening the possibility for one Defence case to follow the other, so we'd have a little more time. We will, of course, in line with what Mr. Stein has said, try and keep track of what they're doing, but I can't be held accountable for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, can you tell us, bearing in mind all the arguments that you have presented, the more limited, smaller team that you have, could you tell us when you could submit your own list of witnesses and your own summaries, could you tell us that? Even if it is a little later, but not too much later, because, of course, we have to know in advance what is your own list of witnesses and your summaries so as to see how the defence should be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite frank with you, Your Honour, I can give you a very rough approximation which will not mean much to you. Why? Because the case has still not been completed for us, and especially if we proceed one after another. May I use an example. We frequently had witnesses who were cross-examined, and you always asked me "How much time do you need?" and I said quite sincerely that I didn't know, because I didn't know whether questions on my list would be asked by my colleague. All of us lawyers often borrow from one another, and he asked many of my own questions; often, he did not. You are familiar with the case, just as I am. There are parts in which the interests of the two Defences quite coincide and there are other parts where our positions are different. If I were to try to give you a rough estimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- may I just have a few more words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you're going to give us a rough estimate, yes, but nothing else because we have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My rough estimate, on the assumption that the Kordic Defence has presented evidence regarding all the background issues - international armed conflict; the question of sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather, the question whether the state fulfils the prerogatives of authority; that is, the reasons for the foundation and existence of the HZ HB; the question of isolation of Central Bosnia, general things like that - and if I consider the Kordic Defence to have done a good job in that area, then I think we could reduce the number to some 50 to 70 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fifty to seventy? After a hundred witnesses for the other accused? If there are a hundred witnesses, which was the figure we heard at one stage, as I recollect, from Mr. Stein - I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - you're not proposing to call another 50 to 70, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is very difficult to estimate because I don't know to what extent we will coincide, except in this area that I have just mentioned. If he, with his witnesses, the other Defence, proffers evidence in a satisfactory manner, and if I am left simply with Vitez and the front line - I'm simplifying things, of course - and a few minor events in Vitez, then, of course, the number will be more restricted, but I can't do any better than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, what is your approximate date? That is all the more reason for you to give us a list of witnesses and summaries so that we can make our own assessment, because, as you can imagine, this trial must be ended within a reasonable time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think two things are needed for realistic planning. To begin with, the Prosecution must complete its case, or we must know these are the Prosecution witnesses, these are the transcripts which are admitted and which are not and how many of them, and then Kordic's defence. If we proceed in the manner you suggested, that first Kordic's Defence presents its tentative list. Then I will say, "Yes. Right. So I do not need this, that, and so on and so forth." And after that, if I decide that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how long -- how long after the submission of the list by of Kordic, how long will it then take you to prepare your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think not more than 10 days. But not the summaries, though. That would be difficult. I should like to add two minor things also. First, as for the summaries, if I may suggest the following: When we're preparing the list of witnesses with summaries, why can't we merely outline the subject, the matter on which the witness is to testify? Because on the basis of that, Your Honours can decide whether that particular witness is relevant or not. So all we say is in one sentence: This witness will testify about, say, conflict in Old Vitez, in Stari Vitez, in April 1993, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's insufficient, because that's not going to give either the Prosecution or the Court a notion of what they're going to say, and more precision is necessary in order to explain what it is about a particular subject that the witness is going to say. That is the important part. Mr. Kovacic, we'll consider things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. Just one brief matter, and I do apologise. In the light of what you said, that we would have a conference under Rule 73 ter, judging by what you said in the beginning, Mr. President, you presumably mean 73 ter of July 1999. But meanwhile, there was yet another revision in November, but I know that you're referring to the one of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I said we were going to proceed on the old Rules, which seem to apply to this case. There is no Pre-Trial Judge, which is what that Rule, the newer version, has in mind and anticipates. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only two things arising from what's been said about the summaries. I've made my argument. There is, in fact, nothing to stop the service of statements if the Defence so choose. There is no need for the thing to be boiled down. If they want to serve the statements, they can serve the statements, and then we will be in a position to decide whether to agree that they should be read, and the Chamber will be in a proper position to deal with the list. The form of summaries proposed by either defendant will simply not enable us to allow material to be read and will not enable us to avoid the attendance of witnesses. Ms. Verhaag has arrived and is able to point us to the source where we should be able to give you the precedent of an order made in another Chamber. It may be as I've described it; who knows. It may not be, because what you're told along a corridor is not always as reliable as seeing the actual document. What I've been told is what I've explained to you, and I'd like you to have the chance to consider that if we can find it first. I think that's really all I need say on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: For the Court's edification, there is no witness statement in our possession. We don't do the work the way they do. We don't send investigators into the field armed with tape recorders and typewriters to take formal statements. There is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the motion for judgement of acquittal is concerned, the Rules apply, and we'll certainly consider the application made by the Defence, provided there is a proper motion put in. By a "proper motion," I mean it doesn't have to be vastly detailed, but it has to indicate what the point is in each case, and we would allow such a motion to be put in if the seven days is longer than was anticipated, with the thing ending on the -- Prosecution ending on the 10th of March. The Prosecution, if we haven't said so, will have seven days to reply, and on the 30th of March we'll have an oral hearing. And working on the basis that the brief provided by the Defence will set out the contested matters, and what is admitted, if anything, we propose to allow the application by the Kordic Defence, that they should set their case out in the way which they propose, with the dates which they propose. It must be understood that the summaries are sufficient for the Court to grasp what it is that the witness will testify about. As far as the Cerkez Defence is concerned, we think balancing the resources which we appreciate are at their disposal, but also having regard to what the Rules require, that the fairest way of dealing with that Defence is to order the various items to be dealt with 14 days after the Kordic Defence. So the order will apply to them mutatis mutandis, as the Latinists say, 14 days later. We are of the view that this courtroom is no longer tolerable for sitting in, so we're going to move, and Courtroom I will be available tomorrow. Anything else? It's now 25 to 5, and I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Two points for the Court to consider. The first, most important, I believe, to the smooth running of the case, is the order of cross-examination of the Kordic witnesses that we put on. I presume the Prosecution will cross-examine first. There appears to be a disagreement within this courthouse as to whether the other defendant gets to cross-examine at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would have presumed otherwise, that Mr. Cerkez would cross-examine first, then the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, that, I guess, needs to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then you re-examine, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That part I was aware of, just who goes first. The next issue, Your Honours, is the issue of the opening statement. We will make our opening statement, of course, on April 10. I don't believe, if I understand the Court's position, that the Cerkez Defence will go after us, although perhaps you have in mind that they will make their opening next. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. From time to time, Your Honours, taking a lead from my learned colleague in the Prosecution, we will be presenting to the Court creative ideas to shorten this trial, but I won't burden the Court with any of those now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I meant to mention earlier, I've once been -- been one other case in this place, and there the Defence read 73(B)(iii)(a) as allowing them to list their witnesses by pseudonym. The matter then had to be readdressed so that they were compelled to give the witnesses by name, save, of course, where there's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other thing that I desire to say -- I'm sorry, it's -- well, I think we've got the possibility of an ex parte hearing, but it looks like not tonight. I hope it can be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Find a convenient time. I mean, it may be before the luncheon adjournment. The difficulty is that we all have to rise and the tapes have to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand. The other thing that I was going to mention at some stage, and I really must mention it now because I may want to refer to this in another setting tomorrow afternoon or tomorrow evening, where not all the parties here will have even ears to hear, and it's this: We've had three village witnesses this week. I've noted the cross-examination following on from the complete refusal to admit anything in this case, despite documents served two years ago and more, and summaries served two years ago and more. I've noticed the distress caused to at least one of those witnesses, and I venture, respectfully, to draw to the Court's attention that this approach to having everything proved, which has been the clarion call of the Defence, not only leads to inefficiency, in my respectful submission, making the approach we proposed, as I saw Judge Robinson was to say in a speech at Leiden University, something that would, had it been possible to accept it, the greatest, most effective improvement in procedure, were it possible, which we quite respect wasn't possible, but that method would also have saved distress to witnesses, and I regret what's happened this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You called the witnesses, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We had to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
